claims.text: A nanoscale conformal TiN or similar carbide/nitride coating on tungsten particles will reduce thermal boundary resistance at the W–Cu interface.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
The coating will improve metallurgical bonding between tungsten particles and the copper matrix.
The coating will reduce interfacial lattice mismatch between tungsten and copper.
Reduced lattice mismatch will minimize phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
A robust metallurgical bond at the coated interface will improve thermal conduction.
The coating's inherent stability will provide a barrier to irradiation-induced damage.
Suppressing irradiation-induced damage at the interface will preserve mechanical strength.
Magnetron sputtering can be used to coat reinforcing particles before composite fabrication.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the uncoated control.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the uncoated control.
The predicted improvement will persist under high thermal loads and neutron irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joints.
The predicted benefit requires the coating to be uniform and optimized in thickness and composition.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement may depend on coating material, thickness, and uniformity.
Long-term performance of the proposed coated W–Cu composite under sustained irradiation has not been fully quantified.
